Title: Population growth rate on the decline
NewsSummary: A Conference on Pakistan's Population Issues in the 21st Century took place this week in Karachi. It was sponsored jointly by the Population Council and Aga Khan University (AKU).

content.text: A Conference on Pakistan's Population Issues in the 21st Century took place this week in Karachi. It was sponsored jointly by the Population Council and Aga Khan University (AKU). The three-day meeting covered a wide range of population issues, such as the 1998 Census, Population and Development, Migration and Urbanization, Reproductive Health, Maternal and Infant Mortality, Fertility and Family Planning and Gender Issues. About 200 participants from all over Pakistan and experts from abroad attended the conference; it was also the occasion of the launching of the Population Association of Pakistan. Dr M.S. Jillani was elected unopposed as the President of the Association.

The chief guest, Dr Shahid Amjad Chaudhry, Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission, said in his inaugural address that"the recent decline in the population growth rate from 3.1 to 2.2 would make the task of creating employment and sending children to school much less difficult." He then focused on the government's policies for the social sectors and showed concern for the increasing poverty in the country.

Dr Carner W. Vellani, Rector, AKU, welcomed the participants, and highlighted that the University recognizes population growth as a key issue and has recently established the Reproductive Health Programme as one of its priority research areas.

In his keynote address, Dr Gavin Jones, Convenor, Graduate Programme in Demography, Australian National University, analyzed population growth trends in Pakistan as compared to other Islamic countries. Although Pakistan is finally experiencing a fertility transition, Professor Jones outlined constraints on the speed of this fertility change such as lack of female autonomy and low educational levels. He strongly argued against any religious factor constraining fertility change in Muslim countries generally.

Dr Mehtab Karim, Reproductive Health Programme, AKU, summarized the need and purpose of the Conference. Dr Nizamuddin, Director, Asia and Pacific Division, UNFPA, congratulated the organizers for the extensive programme of the Conference, saying that"Now is the time to act, and this Conference provides a very good beginning."

The first day's proceedings included a Panel discussion on the results of the 1998 Census, including an interactive session with the audience regarding the reliability and quality of the Census findings. The second day focused on abortions as a Public Health issue in Pakistan. Research findings clearly showed that women with large families are resorting to abortions to avoid unwanted pregnancies, rather t tan using family planning to prevent such births. In his paper on Population and Development, Dr John Wall, Resident Representative of the World Bank, discussed trends and outcomes in the social sector. He said that the"vicious cycle of poverty, poor health and low education" must be turned into a "various cycle" through public sector programmes.

On the last day of the conference, in a panel discussion on"Aging as an Emerging Concern", it was emphasised that while aging was not an immediate concern in Pakistan, it would become one in twenty years and it was therefore important to prepare for this eventuality. Dr Franklin White, chairman of Department of Community Health Sciences, AKU, in his concluding remarks highlighting the necessity and immediacy of tackling important population and environmental issues in Pakistan. A consensus was reached that such a conference should be held annually to highlight population related issues in Pakistan.
